newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN COURT SAYS CAN'T HEAR SHIP COLLISION CASE.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN COURT SAYS CAN'T HEAR SHIP COLLISION CASE.

text.p: A Belgian court ruled on Monday it was incompetent to hear a case brought after a collision off the Belgian coast between a Panamanian-registered cargo ship and a British oil tanker in 1993.
"There has been a declaration of incompetence by the court," an official at the court in the northern Belgian town of Bruges told Reuters.

Nine people died in June 1993 when the British Petroleum (BP) tanker British Trent was engulfed in flames after a collision in thick fog with the Panamanian-registered bulk carrier Western Winner off the port of Ostend in one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
The deaths occurred when the crew of the 25,000-tonne Bermuda-registered British Trent were forced to leap from their burning tanker into the sea. None of the crew of the Western Winner was hurt.
Following a two-month probe the Western Winnner's captain, 50-year-old South Korean Dae Pung Gang, was charged in December 1993 with unintentional killing and with breaking shipping rules.
The shipowners, Liberia-based Alpha Beta Investment, are held civilly responsible on the same charges.
A 1952 international treaty on shipping accidents states that only a court or authority of the country under whose flag the ship is sailing -- Panama -- could handle the case.

One of the articles of the treaty states that such cases could also be handled in the country in whose territorial waters the accident occurred. But the official said Belgium had failed to ratify that article.
The Bruges public prosecutor's office has 15 days to appeal against the court ruling and the official said it planned to do so.
He said the captain had disappeared after the accident.
"We were never able to find him," he said. "But this case is more important for the shipowner," he added.
Belgian authorities said in June 1993 that a pilot boat tried for 45 minutes to warn the Western Winner it was dangerously close to the petrol-laden British Trent.

At the time of the accident, both ships were setting down or picking up a pilot. The pilots con ships through the narrow sea lanes and up the Scheldt river to the ports of Antwerp in Belgium and Flushing in the Netherlands.
About 150 vessels pass through the shipping lane every day.

A report by Britain's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) last year said the Western Winner's captain was unfamiliar with the area where the collision occurred and the vessel was not proceeding "at a safe speed".
The 30,000-tonne bulk carrier had not kept an effective look-out and did not make proper use of its radar given the foggy conditions, the report said.
It added that the British Trent also failed to make proper use of its radar.
